title: Linked lists
summary: Splice a known node in O(1); reaching index i is O(n).

parts.rule: A linked list stores value plus a pointer to the next node. Splicing at a known node is O(1) pointer rewrites. Reaching index i walks i nodes, so that is O(n). Prefer a dummy head when deletes can hit the first node, and draw the pointers before coding.
parts.why: Prompts that say "reorder nodes" or "remove the nth from end" tempt an array mindset. If you convert to an array you pay extra space and miss the pointer skill the interviewer wants. The common bug is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite next without saving it.
parts.example: List 1→2→3→4→5, remove the node with value 3 when you already hold a pointer to node 2. Save node3.next (4). Set node2.next = 4. Node 3 is detached. The list is 1→2→4→5. Cost: two pointer writes, no scan. Now remove the 2nd from end without knowing length: place fast two steps ahead of slow on a dummy→1→2→4→5. Advance both until fast hits the end; slow sits before the victim. Relink slow.next = slow.next.next. You never computed length up front; the gap of two enforced the distance.
parts.use: Use a linked list when you splice, reverse, or merge sequences and you already hold the node handles. Use it for LRU-style structures paired with a hash map of node pointers. Use a dummy head when the head itself may be deleted or replaced.
parts.refuse: Refuse a linked list when the hot path is random index access. Refuse claiming O(1) access to the k-th element. Refuse mutating next without keeping a reference to the remainder. Refuse converting the whole list to an array "for ease" when the point of the prompt is pointer manipulation.

body:
Rule. A linked list stores value plus a pointer to the next node. Splicing at a known node is O(1) pointer rewrites. Reaching index i walks i nodes, so that is O(n). Prefer a dummy head when deletes can hit the first node, and draw the pointers before coding.

Why it matters. Prompts that say "reorder nodes" or "remove the nth from end" tempt an array mindset. If you convert to an array you pay extra space and miss the pointer skill the interviewer wants. The common bug is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite next without saving it.

Worked example. List 1→2→3→4→5, remove the node with value 3 when you already hold a pointer to node 2. Save node3.next (4). Set node2.next = 4. Node 3 is detached. The list is 1→2→4→5. Cost: two pointer writes, no scan. Now remove the 2nd from end without knowing length: place fast two steps ahead of slow on a dummy→1→2→4→5. Advance both until fast hits the end; slow sits before the victim. Relink slow.next = slow.next.next. You never computed length up front; the gap of two enforced the distance.

When to use. Use a linked list when you splice, reverse, or merge sequences and you already hold the node handles. Use it for LRU-style structures paired with a hash map of node pointers. Use a dummy head when the head itself may be deleted or replaced.

When to refuse. Refuse a linked list when the hot path is random index access. Refuse claiming O(1) access to the k-th element. Refuse mutating next without keeping a reference to the remainder. Refuse converting the whole list to an array "for ease" when the point of the prompt is pointer manipulation.
